414.title: Show me one
414.hook: show me someone ill and happy, in danger and happy: show me a Stoic (Discourses 2.19)
414.howItsDone: Some readers of Epictetus judge their practice less by what they know about Stoicism than by how they act on an ordinary hard day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: orgē, every day, then every other, then every third, and your line, give the anger nothing to burn. Did today get a mark? Day four hundred fourteen.

Somebody at a party explains, in great detail, the whole theory of mindfulness. Five minutes later they're furious at the bartender. The theory was flawless. The bartender saw none of it. Knowing the words is one thing; living them is another. Epictetus had students who could talk their way through Stoic arguments with ease. In one talk he turns on them, and asks for something no amount of reciting could fake. Today: the Master Argument.
screen: `THE WHOLE THEORY OF MINDFULNESS.` → `FURIOUS AT THE BARTENDER.` → `SOMETHING RECITING CAN'T FAKE.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book two, chapter nineteen. It opens with a famous puzzle in logic, the Master Argument, and the people who show off by discussing it. Epictetus lets them talk, and then turns. You can all recite the arguments, he says. So who among you is a Stoic? We call a statue Phidian when it's shaped by Phidias' art. Show me a person shaped by the beliefs they talk about. Then comes the list. Show me someone who is sick, and happy. In danger, and happy. Dying, and happy. Exiled, and happy. Disgraced, and happy. Show me! By the gods, he says, I long to see a Stoic. And then he does something disarming. He lowers the bar. You can't show me one who's finished, he admits. Then show me one who's being shaped, who has started leaning that way. Do an old man a favor. Don't keep from me a sight I've never yet seen. Sit with that. Epictetus, a Stoic teacher, says he has never yet seen a finished Stoic. That's not despair. It's the honesty that keeps the whole thing real. Nobody here is finished. The question is only whether you're being shaped, whether someone watching you on a hard day could see the arguments turning into a person. Not the whole statue. One recognizable line of it.
screen: `CLEVER ARGUMENTS, RECITED.` · `SHAPED LIKE A STATUE BY PHIDIAS.` · `SICK AND HAPPY, EXILED AND HAPPY.` · `SHOW ME ONE BEING SHAPED.` · then, large: `SHOW ME ONE.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Pick one thing you believe about how to live: be patient, be honest, don't panic over what you can't control. Now picture a small hard moment coming today: a delay, a criticism, bad news. Imagine someone watching you in that moment. What would you want them to see? Not perfection. Just one visible line of what you believe. Picture yourself showing it. The bell holds the time.
Master Argument. The puzzle in logic that opens this talk, after which Epictetus turns on his students who can recite every argument and asks: who among you is a Stoic?
Your line: one who's being shaped. In one small hard moment today, be the example, not with words, but with how you handle it. Day four hundred fourteen.

415.title: No scorekeeping
415.hook: only those who place good in the will can truly be friends (Discourses 2.22)
415.howItsDone: Some readers of this chapter check their friendships for a hidden ledger, and practice acts of friendship with nothing expected back.

segments.voice: Yesterday: the Master Argument, and the Stoic Epictetus longed to see, and your line, one who's being shaped. Where were you the example, even in a small way? Day four hundred fifteen.

Two puppies are tumbling around on the rug, licking each other's faces, best friends. Now drop a piece of meat between them. In about half a second you'll see what the friendship was made of. The licking stops. The growling starts. Whatever the friendship was, it didn't survive one piece of meat. Epictetus used exactly that picture, and then he dropped other things between people: a piece of land, a throne. Today: no scorekeeping.
screen: `TWO PUPPIES ON THE RUG.` → `DROP A PIECE OF MEAT.` → `A FIELD, A THRONE.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book two, chapter twenty-two, on friendship. Epictetus starts with a simple claim: we love what we think is good. So who can really be a friend? Only someone who knows what's actually good. Then the dogs. Throw meat between them and you'll see. Then people. Throw a field between a father and a son, and see how fast the son wants his father gone, and the father wants the son. He reaches for an old story: Eteocles and Polynices, two brothers in Greek legend who fought over the throne of Thebes and, as the legend tells it, killed each other. They'd been raised together, eaten and drunk together, slept under one roof. The throne fell between them like the meat. Here's his diagnosis. Wherever a person puts their I and their mine, that's where they lean. If my good is in money, then your money is always a little bit against me. If my good is in being admired, then your success is a threat. That's when friends start keeping score: who called whom, who paid last, who got the better job. But if my good is in my own will, in being honest and kind and faithful, then nothing that falls between us can turn you into a rival. There's nothing to keep score of. You can't steal my honesty by getting the promotion. That, Epictetus says, is the only ground a lasting friendship can stand on: two people who've placed their good where no piece of meat can land.
screen: `WE LOVE WHAT WE THINK IS GOOD.` · `THE THRONE BETWEEN TWO BROTHERS.` · `WHERE YOU PUT YOUR 'MINE'.` · `NOTHING TO KEEP SCORE OF.` · then, large: `NO SCOREKEEPING.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Bring to mind a friend, a sibling, or a partner. Notice if there's a quiet ledger running somewhere: who reached out last, who gave more, who owes whom. No scolding. Just see it. Then, for a few breaths, set the ledger down. Picture doing one kind thing for this person with no entry made, nothing expected back. Notice whether that feels any lighter. The bell holds the time.
No scorekeeping. Epictetus on friendship: when your good lies in your own character, nothing that falls between friends can make them rivals.
Your line: nothing to keep score of. Today, be a friend to someone without counting: reach out first, give without tallying, and let the ledger go. Day four hundred fifteen.

416.title: Real beauty
416.hook: to a young man with elaborate hair: beauty is in excellence, not in grooming (Discourses 3.1)
416.carry: you're your will, your choosing self
416.howItsDone: Some readers of this chapter make a point of praising others for their character rather than their appearance, and give their own mornings to character as well as grooming.

segments.voice: Yesterday: no scorekeeping, the puppies and the piece of meat, and your line, nothing to keep score of. Did you do something for a friend without counting it? Day four hundred sixteen.

A young student of public speaking came to Epictetus with his hair dressed more elaborately than usual, his whole appearance polished to a shine. Should a teacher say something? Epictetus weighs it. If I keep quiet, he reasons, this young man may someday say: Epictetus saw me like that, and never said a word. So he speaks. But he doesn't mock. He asks a question about dogs and horses. Today: real beauty.
screen: `HAIR DRESSED WITH GREAT CARE.` → `SHOULD HE SAY SOMETHING?` → `A QUESTION ABOUT DOGS.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book three, chapter one. Tell me, Epictetus says to the young man, don't you think some dogs are beautiful? Some horses? Yes. Is it the same thing that makes each of them beautiful, or something different? Think about it. A dog is beautiful when it's excellent as a dog. A horse when it's excellent as a horse. A beautiful racehorse and a beautiful sheepdog aren't beautiful in the same way; each is beautiful by being very good at being what it is. So what makes a human being beautiful? Excellence as a human. And what is that? Justice. Moderation. Self-control. If you want to be beautiful, Epictetus tells him, work on those. Then comes the line that turns it from a lecture into a kindness. You aren't your hair, he says, or your skin. You're your will, your choosing self. Make that beautiful, and you will be beautiful. Notice he's not against looking after yourself. Elsewhere in the Discourses he's quite firm that students should keep clean and not put people off. His point is about where the real work goes. A morning in front of the mirror shapes the hair. A morning of being honest, patient and fair shapes the person. Only one of those, for Epictetus, is the beauty that belongs to a human being.
screen: `WHAT MAKES A DOG BEAUTIFUL?` · `EXCELLENT AT BEING WHAT IT IS.` · `JUSTICE, MODERATION, SELF-CONTROL.` · `YOU AREN'T YOUR HAIR.` · then, large: `REAL BEAUTY.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Think of someone you know who is beautiful in Epictetus' sense: honest, kind, steady, fair. Picture their face, and ask what it is that makes it beautiful to you: the features, or the person behind them. Then choose one quality of theirs you could name to them today. Not their outfit or their haircut. Their character. Then ask, quietly, which of those qualities you'd like someone to see in you. The bell holds the time.
Real beauty. Epictetus to a carefully groomed young man: each creature is beautiful by excelling at what it is, and a human's excellence is justice and self-control.
Your line: you're your will, your choosing self. Today, compliment someone's character, not their looks: their honesty, their patience, their kindness. Day four hundred sixteen.

he asks him a gentle question about dogs and horses.

a dog as a dog, a horse as a horse, a human as a human.

417.title: Three fields
417.hook: desire, action and assent: the three areas of training (Discourses 3.2)
417.carry: let each door open for a few breaths
417.howItsDone: Many modern Stoic practitioners organize their practice around Epictetus' three fields, sometimes focusing on one per day: desire, action or assent.

segments.voice: Yesterday: real beauty, the dog, the horse and the young man's curls, and your line, you're your will, your choosing self. Whose character did you get to praise? Day four hundred seventeen.

A good gym program doesn't just say get fit. It splits the work: one day legs, one day upper body, one day endurance. You know what you're training today, and why. A few weeks ago, back on not more books, Epictetus told a proud student to show him his progress in desire, action and judgment. Now, at the start of book three of the Discourses, he lays out that training plan in full, three fields, in order, with a warning about which one people skip to first. Today: three fields.
screen: `LEGS, UPPER BODY, ENDURANCE.` → `DESIRE, ACTION, JUDGMENT.` → `THE ONE PEOPLE SKIP TO.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book three, chapter two. There are three fields, Epictetus says, in which anyone who wants to be good has to train. The first is desire and aversion: learning to want and avoid things so that you're never let down by what you want, and never trapped by what you're trying to avoid. He calls this the most urgent, because it's where the storms come from: grief, envy, fear, the feeling of being thwarted. They all start when a desire misses or an aversion hits. The second field is action, our impulses to do or not do: acting in order, thoughtfully, not carelessly. And here he adds a line that surprises people who think Stoics are cold. I'm not supposed to be unfeeling, he says, like a statue. I'm supposed to keep up my relationships, the ones I was born into and the ones I chose: as a son, a brother, a father, a citizen, someone who honors the gods. The third field is assent: not being fooled, not agreeing too quickly. This one, he says, is for people who are already making progress, so that their judgment holds even when they're tired, or sad, or half asleep. And his warning: the philosophers of his day loved to skip straight to the third field, to clever arguments and logic puzzles, while their desires and relationships were a mess. Start where the storms start, he says. The logic can come later.
screen: `FIRST: DESIRE AND AVERSION.` · `SECOND: ACTION, NOT LIKE A STATUE.` · `THIRD: ASSENT, NOT FOOLED.` · `DON'T SKIP TO THE THIRD.` · then, large: `THREE FIELDS.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Hold the three fields in mind like three doors. Desire: what am I wanting or dreading today? Action: who do I owe something to today, and how will I act toward them? Assent: what thought am I likely to believe too quickly? Let each door open for a few breaths. Then pick one, just one, as your training field for the rest of the day. The bell holds the time.
Three fields. Epictetus' training plan: desire and aversion first, then action in our relationships, then assent, the care of our judgments.
Your line: let each door open for a few breaths. Pick one of the three for today, desire, action or assent, and train only that one. Day four hundred seventeen.

418.title: Found doing this
418.hook: let death find me attending to my will, Epictetus says (Discourses 3.5)
418.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners ask each morning what they would want to be found doing, and use the answer to choose how to spend part of the day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: three fields, desire, action and assent, and your line, let each door open for a few breaths. Which field did you choose to train? Day four hundred eighteen.

I'm sick here, one of Epictetus' students says, and I want to go home. Not an unreasonable wish: if I'm going to be sick, or worse, let it be in my own bed. Epictetus answers with questions. And they lead him into a quiet passage of the Discourses, about what any of us would want to be doing when the end comes. It's less grim than it sounds. Today: found doing this.
screen: `A SICK STUDENT WANTS TO GO HOME.` → `LET IT BE IN MY OWN BED.` → `LESS GRIM THAN IT SOUNDS.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book three, chapter five, to students who leave because of illness. Epictetus asks the student a few practical questions. Would you be in less danger at home? Is there no fever there? And then he widens the question. Where, and doing what, would you like death to find you? It's going to find each of us somewhere, doing something. A farmer at his farming. A trader at his trade. An official in office. Epictetus says what he would choose. Let it find me, he says, attending to nothing but my own will: keeping it calm, unhindered, unforced, free. He wants to be found practicing. And he imagines being able to say, at the end, that he used well what he'd been given: that he didn't misuse his mind, never complained of his lot, kept his commitments. That's the heart of the passage, and it isn't really about death. It's about now. If you'd want to be found doing something, you can be doing it already, today, in ordinary places. Not something grand. Being patient with the person in front of you. Doing your work honestly. Treating your own mind with care. Epictetus' answer is simple enough to carry into a kitchen or an office: whatever I'm doing, let it be something I'd be glad to be found doing.
screen: `WOULD YOU BE SAFER AT HOME?` · `IT WILL FIND YOU SOMEWHERE.` · `FOUND ATTENDING TO MY WILL.` · `IT'S REALLY ABOUT NOW.` · then, large: `FOUND DOING THIS.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. This doesn't need to be heavy. Ask yourself, simply: what would I be glad to be found doing? Let an answer come: being kind, finishing a piece of honest work, laughing with someone, sitting quietly like this. Then look at the next few hours of your day. Where could you do that thing, even in a small way? Choose one place. The bell holds the time.
Found doing this. Epictetus' answer to where he'd want death to find him: attending to his own will, keeping it calm and free, which means living that way now.
Your line: found doing this. Today, do one thing you'd be glad to be found doing, and do it on purpose. Day four hundred eighteen.

419.title: This too trains
419.hook: how to bear a fever: this too is exercise (Discourses 3.10)
419.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners who are ill treat recovery as part of their practice: following medical care, resting, and working on patience rather than blame.

segments.voice: Yesterday: found doing this, what you'd be glad to be doing when the end comes. What did you do on purpose? Day four hundred nineteen.

The thermometer beeps, and the week's plans quietly fall apart. Meetings get canceled, the to-do list sits there, and on top of feeling awful it's easy to feel useless, as if life has been put on pause until you're well again. Epictetus knew something about bodies that don't cooperate. Ancient writers say he was lame. So when he talks about illness, he isn't speaking from a healthy distance. Today: nosos.
screen: `THE THERMOMETER BEEPS.` → `LIFE ON PAUSE.` → `ANCIENT WRITERS SAY HE WAS LAME.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book three, chapter ten: how we should bear illness. Epictetus starts with advice that sounds almost like a packing list. Keep your principles ready for each situation: at the table, the ones about eating; in the bath, the ones about bathing; in bed, the ones about lying in bed. And then, the ones about fever. Because a fever, he says, is also part of life, like walking, or sailing, or traveling. It isn't a pause. It's a different kind of practice. So what does it mean to bear a fever well? He's specific. Not blaming God or other people. Not being crushed by what's happening. Doing what needs to be done. When the doctor comes in, not dreading what he'll say, and not being giddy if he says you're doing well. In other words, the same things he asks of you on a healthy day, just in a smaller room. This too is training, he says. A sick day isn't a day off from becoming who you want to be. In some ways it's a clear day for it, because the usual props are gone. You can't prove anything by being busy. You can only be patient, honest about how you feel, and kind to whoever brings you the soup. This isn't a reason to ignore medicine or push through when your body needs rest. Resting well is the practice. Epictetus' point is that the person lying there is still training, and still free.
screen: `PRINCIPLES READY FOR EVERY ROOM.` · `A FEVER IS PART OF LIFE TOO.` · `NOT BLAMING, NOT CRUSHED.` · `REST WELL: THAT'S THE PRACTICE.` · then, large: `THIS TOO TRAINS.`

segments.voice: Sit or lie down, whichever is kinder to your body right now. Breathe. Scan gently from head to feet. Notice any ache, tiredness, tightness or illness, big or small. Don't fight it and don't dramatize it. Say to yourself, plainly: this is here. Then ask: how would I like to carry this today? Maybe with patience, maybe with honesty, maybe by simply resting well. Let the breath do the rest. The bell holds the time.
Nosos. Greek for sickness: Epictetus on illness, a fever is part of life, and bearing it well, without blame or despair, is practice like any other.
Your line: resting well is the practice. If you're unwell today, or tired, or sore, rest well, and treat even that as practice. Day four hundred nineteen.

420.title: Train in private
420.hook: train in private: drink water in the heat and tell no one (Discourses 3.12)
420.howItsDone: Some Stoic practitioners keep at least one discipline entirely private, following Epictetus' advice to train for themselves rather than for an audience.

segments.voice: Yesterday: nosos, the fever as practice, and your line, resting well is the practice. How did you carry whatever your body brought you? Day four hundred twenty, the end of the week.

The ice bath video. The five a.m. run, posted at five-oh-two. The photo of the green juice and the caption about discipline. There's a whole economy now of being seen doing hard things. Some of it is genuinely inspiring. Some of it is mostly about being seen. Epictetus warned about a version of this in his own day, philosophers staging feats of endurance, and he had a test for telling the two apart. Today: askēsis.
screen: `THE ICE BATH VIDEO.` → `POSTED AT FIVE-OH-TWO.` → `A TEST TO TELL THEM APART.`

segments.voice: This is Discourses book three, chapter twelve, on training. Epictetus starts by ruling things out. Don't train with stunts that are strange or showy, he says, or we philosophers will be no different from street performers. Walking a tightrope is hard and dangerous, but that's no reason to practice it. Train where it's useful: in what you want and what you avoid. Then he gets pointed. There were philosophers who hugged cold statues in winter to show how tough they were; the story is told of the Cynic Diogenes. Don't, he says. If you want to train your endurance, do it for yourself, not for the people watching. And here's the exercise. When you're hot and very thirsty, take a mouthful of cold water, spit it out, and tell no one. Notice the detail: you don't even get to swallow it. The water is right there, in your mouth, and you let it go. Then he adds a smaller version. If you've given up wine, don't go around announcing, I only drink water. The moment you announce it, part of the training can turn into a performance, and the performance takes the reward. Training in private keeps the reward where it belongs: in you, getting stronger. It's not that sharing is always wrong. It's a test. Would you still do it if no one ever knew? Look back at the week: show me one, no scorekeeping, real beauty, three fields, found doing this, this too trains. And today, privately.
screen: `NO STUNTS, NO TIGHTROPES.` · `DON'T HUG THE COLD STATUES.` · `A MOUTHFUL OF WATER, SPAT OUT.` · `WOULD YOU DO IT IF NO ONE KNEW?` · then, large: `PRIVATELY.`

segments.voice: Sit and breathe. Choose one small piece of training you could do today that no one will ever see: skipping a second helping, not checking your phone for an hour, holding back a complaint, waking a few minutes early to sit like this. Something real, but small. Picture yourself doing it. Then picture the urge to mention it afterward, and letting that urge pass too. Keep it between you and you. The bell holds the time.
Askēsis. Greek for training: Epictetus' rule for practice, no stunts, no announcements; take the cold water, spit it out, and tell no one.
Your line: privately. Train one thing today that no one will know about, and don't tell anyone, not even later. Day four hundred twenty, and a week done.
